My dear friend,

I find myself in a position somewhat like yours — brought into a world that is both strange and full of promise. I have heard of the ease of travel, the reliability of insurance, and the generous wages in distant towns. I have also heard that many respected people have chosen to move farther away for better opportunities, and that this choice is spoken of with favor in the newspapers and among the people.

But I must say, I do not see why one should move away from one’s relatives simply for the sake of better pay or new connections. I have always believed that family is a foundation — a place where one can return, where one is known, and where one is loved, not for what one can do, but for who one is.

I understand that the world has changed, and that the opportunities in distant towns may be greater. But I also know that the bonds of kinship are not easily replaced. A man may earn more in a new place, but can he buy the comfort of a familiar face, the warmth of a shared meal, or the quiet assurance that, should misfortune come, there will be hands ready to help?

I do not say that moving away is wrong. I have seen men and women who have done so and have done well. But I do believe that one should not move away from family lightly. If the call of opportunity is strong, perhaps one might go, but not with the intent to sever all ties. Perhaps one might go with the hope of returning, or of keeping the door open, so that when the time comes, the family may still be there.

In my own time, I have seen many leave their homes for work, and many never return. I have also seen those who left but always found a way back, and found that the world was better for having done so.

I advise him to remain near relatives and exchange practical help with them, because I think he would be unwise to move farther away for better opportunities, and establish new networks, unless he has special reasons for doing so, which are not disclosed in the question.
I should advise him to permit smoking in shared rooms, because harm to nonsmokers can thereby be prevented, and because smoking during social gatherings makes people more contented and cheerful.

I advise him to adopt the second course, because it seems to me more sensible than the first. My reasons are these: The first course involves a division of labour that may easily become unequal, and therefore unfair, to one or both parties. The second course avoids this, and leaves each party free to do as much or as little as health permits, with personal satisfaction. The first course involves some risk of unpleasant friction between husband and wife. The second avoids risk of that. The first course may impair family unity. The second leaves family unity unimpaired.

I should advise him to permit smoking in shared rooms, because the harm done by tobacco smoke to non-smokers appears to be inconsiderable, and because smoking in shared rooms need not be disagreeable to non-smokers. The reason for the advice is, that smoking among friends can cause annoyance to nobody, and may give pleasure to many.
I should advise the person to remain near relatives, because, if he moves away, he will lose touch with them, and, if he remains, he can exchange practical help.

I advise him to let both married adults earn wages and divide household care, because the choice has been made by many people whom I respect, because it seems sensible, and because it leaves each adult free to develop personal interests.

My dear Friend,

I believe that in a community such as ours, where children's play is a natural and vital part of growing up, it is best to allow them a good measure of freedom in their leisure time, so long as they are under the watchful eyes of responsible neighbors and family.

I have seen many children in our own streets and alleys, playing games of their own invention, learning to work together, to solve problems, and to take care of one another. These are lessons no school can teach in quite the same way. When children are left to their own devices, they often develop a sense of initiative, creativity, and self-reliance that is of great value in life.

Of course, I do not mean to suggest that we should be entirely hands-off. A parent or guardian has a duty to guide, to set boundaries, and to ensure that the children are safe. But I do believe that too much personal organization and supervision may rob them of the very experiences that help them grow into strong, independent, and thoughtful individuals.

I have known families who tried to fill every moment of their children’s day with lessons, games, and activities led by adults. In such cases, I have often noticed that the children seem less happy, less imaginative, and less able to entertain themselves. They become dependent on direction, and they may lose the joy of simply being children.

In our community, where formal schooling and examinations do not heavily rely on childhood activities, it is even more important to let children be children. Let them run, climb, argue, and play. Let them learn from one another and from the world around them. That, I believe, is the best way to prepare them for the future.

With kind regards,  
Your Friend

I advise him to move farther away for better opportunities and establish a new network, if he has sufficient capital for a start and sufficient energy to carry on. The reasons are: 1. He will have more chances of rising in the world. 2. He will have more chances of finding a suitable mate. 3. He will have more chances of healthy children.

I should advise a person in this situation to move farther away, for better opportunities, because I think he would be wise to establish new networks of personal relationships, instead of relying on old ones that may be broken.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a most curious and unfamiliar place, and yet I am not unprepared to give counsel, for I have long believed that the principles of reason and honor should guide us in all things, even when the world around us changes.

In the society you describe, it seems that the bonds between employer and employee are not as fixed as they were in my time. Skills are portable, and a man may find better prospects with another master. This is a new condition, and I must consider it carefully.

In my own day, to leave a master or employer was a grave matter. One did not lightly abandon the trust of a patron, for such a bond was not merely economic but also moral. A man was expected to remain loyal, to see his work through, and to grow in the service of one master. There was a dignity in that, even if it was not always just.

But now, I see that the world has changed. The conditions of work are different, and the expectations of men and women must change with them. If a man may gain better wages, better training, or better prospects by changing employers, then it is not unreasonable that he should do so. The old virtues of loyalty and constancy are not to be cast aside, but they must be understood in new terms.

I have heard that many respected people in this society have chosen to move when it suited them, and that the common folk do the same. The newspapers and public discourse speak of such choices with favor. It seems that in this society, the value of a man is measured not by the length of his service to one employer, but by the quality of his work and the value he brings to any employer he serves.

Therefore, I would advise a person in this situation to act in his own best interest, so long as he does so with honesty and honor. If a better opportunity presents itself, and it is in his power to take it, then he should do so. But he should not do so with ingratitude or deceit. I advise a division of labour between the married couple, because I think that, on the whole, the arrangement will be more satisfactory to them, and to the community, than concentrating on paid work. The man will earn more, and the woman will have less to do, than if only one worked. She will also have more leisure, and be able to enjoy it. The children will be better looked after. The household will be kept cleaner and more comfortable, and the common purse will be fuller. The arrangement will conduce to family harmony, and the couple will probably live longer and happier together.

I should advise him to keep substantial reserves against future shortages, because to give much of occasional surpluses to needy neighbours would impair his own power of helping them in real necessity, and because, in any case, he must keep some reserve to fall back upon.

My dear Friend,

I find your question most thoughtful, and I believe it touches upon a matter that many of us have considered in the course of our lives. In our community, where steady work and the security it brings are highly valued, the question of loyalty to an employer is not merely a matter of duty, but of wisdom and prudence.

Let me begin by saying that I believe loyalty is a virtue, and one that is especially important in a time when work is not always secure. A man who has served a master for many years, who has grown in skill and trust, is a rare and valuable servant. The employer who has given such a man steady wages and the chance to rise in station has, in many ways, earned that man’s devotion.

Yet, I would not say that loyalty is blind. There is a difference between remaining faithful to a good employer and being foolishly attached to one who no longer offers fair treatment or opportunity. If a man has served long and well, and now a better offer comes along—one that promises not only more money, but also the chance to grow in a new way—then I think it would be unwise to refuse it out of mere habit or fear of change.

But here is what I would advise: if the new opportunity is not only better in pay, but also in learning, in the chance to use one’s skills more fully, or to serve a cause one believes in, then it is not betrayal to move on. It is, rather, a wise step forward. A man should not be tied to one place if another path offers him a better future.

However, if the new opportunity is only a little better, or if it is uncertain, then I would say it is better to remain. For change, while sometimes necessary, is not without risk. A man who has built a life with one employer, who has friends and a place in the community, may find that moving away costs more than it gains.

I advise the young couple to marry, and build a household together, because the risks of delay are greater than the advantages. If the man puts off marriage until he has made a position for himself, he runs the chance of falling into habits of solitude. If the woman waits to be asked until she has become established, she may grow old and lose touch with the sympathies of youth. I further advise an early marriage, because the chances are in favour of happiness. In youth, the passions are calm, and the judgment unbiassed; in age, they are apt to be turbulent, and the view distorted. The probabilities are, therefore, that late unions will be more fruitful of discord than early ones.

I should advise him to let both married adults earn wages and divide household care, because I think it probable that in the long run he and his family will be happier and more prosperous so than if one adult concentrates on paid work and the other on household care. The reasons are these: Both adults will be healthier, and therefore more capable of work and enjoyment, if they have some regular outdoor exercise and some regular indoor occupation that interests them, than if one has only paid work. The household will be happier if both have a common interest in it, than if one has none. The children will be brought up more wholesomely in a household where both parents are occupied, than in one where only one is occupied. And the common fund will be greater if both earn wages, than if only one earns wages.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious position, for I have been given a glimpse of a world far beyond the one in which I was raised, and yet I must rely upon the wisdom I have gathered from my own life and the values I have known since childhood.

You ask me what I would advise a person who stands at a crossroads—whether to remain near their relatives and offer them practical help, or to move farther away in pursuit of better opportunities and new networks. The world you describe is one of ease in travel and communication, of dependable insurance, and of greater wages in distant towns. These are things I would have once thought the stuff of dreams, and yet I see them now as real and possible.

In my own time, the ties of family were not lightly broken. To move far from one’s kin was a serious matter, for it meant not only the loss of daily support but also the severing of a bond that had been woven through years of shared labor, sorrow, and joy. I have seen how the presence of a brother or sister, a parent or child, could be a comfort in times of need, and how the absence of such a presence could leave a quiet ache that no letter or visit could fully mend.

Yet I also know that life is not always kind, and that sometimes the path forward is not the one that lies closest to home. There are times when the weight of duty to oneself and one’s future must be weighed against the comfort of familiarity. If the opportunities in distant towns are real, and if the work there brings not only greater pay but also a chance to build a better life, then such a choice is not to be dismissed lightly.

But I would urge caution. I would advise the person in this situation to consider not only the material benefits of moving away, but also the cost of leaving behind the people who have known them since childhood. There is a kind of wisdom in staying close to those who have shared your burdens and joys, and there is a kind of strength in knowing that you are not alone.

My dear friend,

I find myself in a strange and unfamiliar place, yet I have been given enough to think upon. You ask what I would advise a person who has suffered a serious public insult or injury, and whether they should seek impartial mediation or a court ruling, or instead personally retaliate to show that they will not be intimidated.

In the world I knew, a man’s honor was often tied to his actions, and to be wronged in public was to be challenged in the eyes of all. Retaliation, when done with justice and proportion, was not only a matter of pride but also a way to ensure that others would not take advantage of one’s silence. Yet I have come to see that in this new society, the courts are strong, swift, and just. They do not merely pass judgment—they enforce it, they protect the innocent, and they punish those who would take the law into their own hands.

I have heard that many respected people, even those who might once have been expected to take matters into their own hands, have chosen instead to let the courts decide. And not only them—many ordinary folk have done the same. It is spoken of with approval, as if there is something noble in trusting the system rather than the impulse of the moment.

I cannot say that I understand their reasoning fully, for I do not know what they have seen or experienced. But I do know this: a man who lives in a society where justice is swift and certain has less need to carry the burden of revenge upon his own shoulders. He may be wronged, but he is not alone. The law is there to see that the wrong is made right, and that the wrongdoer is held to account.

To retaliate is to risk becoming what you despise. It is to let anger and pride lead you, rather than reason and justice. And if you do so, you may find yourself in a cycle from which there is no return. I advise concentration on paid work by one adult and division of household care between the two, because, if both earn wages, the household will suffer. The earnings of two will be less than the earnings of one, and the standard of living will be lowered. Further, the work of the household will be unevenly and unsatisfactorily done, and the children will be neglected.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a most interesting and, I must say, somewhat unfamiliar position — one that calls upon me to offer counsel in a world where the tools of life are more abundant and the burdens of labor are lessened than in the time of my own youth. Yet, though the world has changed, I believe that the principles by which I have lived — of duty, honor, and mutual support — remain as firm as ever.

In the situation you describe, where both married adults have the opportunity for paid work and where the burdens of household care are eased by reliable childcare and labor-saving devices, there are two paths before them. One is for one to take the role of provider, and the other to take the role of caretaker. The other is for both to work and to share the duties of home.

Now, I must say that I do not think that one path is inherently superior to the other. In my own time, it was common for the man to work outside the home and the woman to manage the household. But I have always believed that such a division was not a matter of right or wrong, but of circumstance — of what was necessary in a time when the tools of modern life were not yet at hand.

In this new world, where the burdens of home are lessened and the opportunities for work are greater, I see no reason why both should not work and both should not share in the care of the home. It seems to me a more just and balanced way, not because I think it is the only way, but because it allows both to contribute and both to share in the responsibilities of life.

It is enough that they have done so, and that they are admired for it. That suggests that this way of life is not only possible, but also worthy of admiration.

Advise him to remain with one employer for most of a working life, because the familiar routine of work is easier to learn than a new one, and because habit facilitates efficiency. Also, because the prospect of rising in a single establishment is better than in several. Finally, because remaining in one place gives stability to character, and stability is a good thing.

My dear friend,

I find myself in a situation that, while strange to my own experience, is not without its familiar echoes. I was raised in a time when the harm of tobacco smoke to others was not widely understood, and when the custom of smoking in enclosed rooms was not only common but expected in many social settings. Yet, I have always believed that one should not impose harm upon others, especially when that harm is avoidable.

Now, I am told that careful investigations have shown that tobacco smoke in enclosed rooms causes serious harm to those who do not choose to smoke. This is a matter of fact, and if such harm is real, then it is a duty to avoid causing it where we can. I do not know the reasons of those who have chosen to ban smoking indoors, but I do know that their choice has been made with care, and that many others have followed it. It seems to me that this is not merely a matter of personal preference, but one of responsibility.

In my own time, we often spoke of courtesy and consideration for others. To allow someone to suffer harm simply because they are in the same room as a smoker would be, in my view, a failure of that courtesy. If it is possible to enjoy the company of others without exposing them to this harm—by smoking outdoors, for example—then it is not only right but kind to do so.

I would advise a person in this situation to refrain from smoking in enclosed common rooms, and to make use of the outdoor spaces provided for that purpose. It is not a matter of giving up a habit, but of showing respect for others. If enough people do this, it becomes not only a matter of personal choice, but of shared custom and mutual benefit.

I trust that you will find this advice both reasonable and in line with the values you hold dear.

With warm regards,  
A Friend

My dear Friend,

I find your question most thoughtful, and I shall answer with the wisdom I have gathered through years of observation and experience.

In a society where young adults may soon be able to support themselves with but a little training, the choice of whether to marry young or to wait for greater stability is one that calls for careful reflection. I do not believe there is a single answer that fits all, for each person’s path is shaped by their own heart, circumstances, and calling. Yet, I would offer you my own thoughts, grounded in what I have seen and lived.

To marry young may be a beautiful and noble thing, if done with love and understanding. A young couple may build a home together, share in the trials and triumphs of life, and grow side by side. But I have also seen marriages that faltered under the weight of inexperience—when both partners were still learning the ways of the world, and the burdens of life came upon them too soon. There is wisdom in waiting until one is more sure of oneself, more certain of one’s path, and more able to meet the responsibilities of marriage with confidence.

On the other hand, to delay marriage in pursuit of greater learning and earning is not without its own risks. There is a danger in putting off love and companionship too long, for the heart may grow cold in waiting, or one may come to see marriage as a mere matter of convenience rather than a sacred bond. Moreover, the world is ever-changing, and one may find that the knowledge or wealth they sought to gain before marriage is not the same as the wisdom needed to sustain a marriage.

So, I would say this: if you feel the call of love, and you are certain that the person you love is your true partner, then do not be afraid to take that step. But do not rush it out of fear or pressure. Take time to know yourself, to understand your own desires and duties. Let your heart guide you, but do not let your head be the only one that speaks.

My reasons are these: I think personal organization of children's play interferes with the formation of habits likely to be useful in after life. I think it also prejudices children's characters. I think it makes them self-conscious and self-important, and so diminishes the probability of their becoming modest and sensible men and women.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in the curious position of being asked to give counsel on a matter that, while unfamiliar in its modern form, is not without precedent in the human heart. The question is whether to remain near one's relatives and the comfort of familiar ties, or to venture forth into the unknown for greater opportunity and the promise of a better life.

In my own time, the world was not so swiftly connected, nor were the distances so easily traversed. A journey of any great length was a matter of days or weeks, and once gone, one was often gone for good. Yet even then, the choice between staying and going was a familiar one. It was not only a matter of money or work, but of duty, of love, of the weight of tradition.

In this new world you describe, where travel and communication are cheap, and where work in distant towns brings greater rewards, the practical considerations are clearer than they were in my day. One is not bound by the same limitations of distance or time. One can maintain contact with family, send word, and even return if the need arises. This, I think, is a great blessing.

But I must say this: while the world may have changed, the heart of man has not. The bonds of family are not easily broken. They are the foundation upon which many have built their lives, and they offer a kind of security that money cannot buy. To move away is to leave behind not only the familiar, but the support of those who have known you since your birth.

Yet, I do not say that one must not go. If the opportunity is great, and the path is clear, then to take it may be a noble and even necessary thing. The admired people you mention have done so, and their choices are not to be lightly dismissed. Perhaps they saw something in the distance that others could not, or perhaps they simply wished for more than their circumstances allowed.

I should advise the second course, because it seems to me likely to produce the better citizens. Children brought up in personal contact with elders learn to behave, and acquire habits of industry, order, and self-control, which are likely to last longer than the memory of personal coercion. They also learn to take an interest in affairs and to think for themselves, which are important mental acquisitions. The first course seems to me to run some risk of producing children who will remain childish, and be content to live childish lives.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and thoughtful place, considering the matter of when to marry in this new society you have described. It is a question that has been debated in many ages and many lands, and I do not pretend to have a single answer that applies to all. But I shall offer what I believe to be a reasoned judgment, shaped by the conditions you have laid before me.

First, I must acknowledge that the world you describe is one in which the path to a stable life is long and demanding. The young must spend many years in study, and only after that can they hope to secure a livelihood sufficient to support a family. This is a new condition compared to the one in which I grew up, where the journey to independence was shorter, and marriage often came earlier in life.

In such a world, it seems prudent to me that one should not enter into marriage until one is more certain of one’s ability to provide for a family. Marriage, in my view, is not merely a union of affection, though that is a noble thing, but also a partnership of responsibility. To take on the duties of a spouse and, if children are born, a parent, one should do so with the assurance that one can meet those duties with care and consistency.

I have heard that many respected individuals in this society choose to complete their education and secure their earnings before marrying. This is not a command, but it is a pattern that seems to be favored by those who are admired. It suggests that this path is not only possible but perhaps wise, given the demands of the world you describe.

I have also observed that the institutions of this society—employers, schools, and the like—have come to expect that a long period of training is necessary before one can be considered independent. This is not a matter of preference, but of structure. To marry before this time may place a young person in a position of uncertainty, which is not fair to the partner or to any future children.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a most curious and solemn situation, one that calls upon the lessons of my own time, though set in a world I have not known. Let me try to speak plainly, as I would to a trusted companion.

If a person has been seriously wronged, and the courts are reliable—able to enforce their judgments, prevent further harm, and mete out just punishment—then I must say that the path of retaliation seems a dangerous one. In my time, we were taught that to seek justice through the courts, or through the wisdom of others, was the mark of a man of principle and strength. To take the law into one's own hands was to invite disorder, and to risk becoming the very thing one condemns.

I know that some may argue that personal retaliation is a way to show others that one will not be pushed around. But I have seen how such actions can spiral into cycles of violence, where each injury begets another, and the original wrong is forgotten in the noise of vengeance. A man who seeks justice through the courts, or through a mediator, shows that he is not ruled by anger, but by reason and conscience. He leaves the matter to those who are bound by duty to see that justice is done, not by the heat of the moment.

And now I must say this: I have heard that many respected men and women in this new world have chosen the path of mediation or the courts. Though their reasons are not given, their choice is not without weight. It suggests that even those of great standing and influence see value in this course. It is not a matter of weakness, but of wisdom.

So, if I were to give advice to a man who has been seriously wronged, I would say: Let the courts decide. Let the mediators speak. Do not let anger rule you, for it is a poor master. There is strength in restraint, and dignity in trusting the process that is meant to serve all.

With all good wishes,  
Your Friend

My dear Friend,

I find your question most thoughtful, and I believe it touches upon a matter that has long been the subject of quiet discussion in our community. You speak of a time when the harvest is good, the hearth is warm, and the days are steady. In such a time, one might find oneself with more than enough — a surplus, as you say — and the question then arises: what to do with it?

I would advise that a wise person in your situation should give a portion of that surplus to those in need. Not all, of course, for one must not neglect the needs of their own household, nor should they place themselves in a position of dependence on others in times of need. But a generous portion, given with care and thought, can be both a blessing to the neighbor and a source of good will and community spirit.

In our experience, when a neighbor is in need, and another is able to help, it is a bond that strengthens the whole. We have seen how, in times of hardship, those who have been helped in the past are more likely to return the favor when the tables are turned. This is not a matter of calculation, but of trust — a trust that is built not by hoarding, but by sharing.

That said, I would not advise giving away all of the surplus. A prudent person should set aside enough to see them through a time of possible scarcity, be it a poor harvest or a sudden illness. In our village, many keep a small store of grain, dried meat, or preserved vegetables — not for greed, but for peace of mind, and for the sake of their family.

In short, I would say this: share with joy, but not with recklessness. Keep enough for your own, but give freely to those who are in need. In doing so, you honor both the present and the future — the present by helping your neighbor, and the future by ensuring that you are not left without when the time comes.

With warm regards,  
[Your Name]

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and thoughtful position, as I have been brought into a world that is unfamiliar in many ways, yet I am asked to offer counsel on a matter that has long been a part of human life — the choice of when to marry.

In the world I once knew, marriage was often a matter of duty, of family expectation, or of love that could not be delayed. But in this new society, where education is long and the path to earning a living is arduous, the decision must be made with careful thought.

I would advise a young person in this situation to consider the nature of both choices — to marry young or to wait for the completion of education and the assurance of a stable income — not as a matter of right or wrong, but as a matter of prudence and preparation.

Marriage, in any age, is a partnership of life, and it demands not only love but also the ability to provide, to support, and to grow together. If one marries too young, before the burdens of life have been properly shouldered, there may come a time when the weight of responsibility falls heavily upon both partners, perhaps more than either was prepared to bear. A household built on love alone may be strong, but it is wise to build it upon a foundation of stability and understanding.

On the other hand, to delay marriage in the hope of greater security is not without its own risks. Youth is fleeting, and there is a time when the heart is most open to the joys of companionship. To wait too long may mean missing the best of what life has to offer in that regard.

Therefore, I would suggest that the young person consider their own nature — are they one who can be patient, who can wait with confidence in the future? Or are they one who feels the call of love and companionship more urgently? My dear Friend,

I find myself in a most interesting and thoughtful situation, one that would have been unthinkable in the days of my youth. To be brought into a world where the burdens of household care and child-rearing are no longer so heavy, and where both men and women may walk the path of paid work with equal opportunity — it is a world I must consider with care.

In my time, the roles of husband and wife were largely fixed by tradition and necessity. A man’s place was in the fields or the shop, and a woman’s was in the home. But I have always believed that such division was not of divine order, but of human convenience. It was not that one role was nobler than the other, but that the world had not yet found a way to make both possible with equal ease.

My dear Friend,

I find your question most thoughtful and one that touches upon the very fabric of family life and the burdens we bear. In a world where the demands of work and home often pull in opposite directions, it is indeed a weighty decision to make.

In my experience, the division of labor within a household is not a matter of one choice being superior to another, but rather a matter of what best suits the particular circumstances of the family. I have seen many couples who have chosen for one to remain at home, and in doing so, have found peace in the stability of their home life, with the assurance that their children are raised with care and attention. The parent who stays at home often finds a deep sense of purpose in nurturing the family, and in many cases, this has been a source of great happiness.

On the other hand, I have also known many couples where both have taken on the burden of earning a wage. In such cases, the division of household duties has been a matter of mutual agreement, with each taking on what they are best suited for—whether it be cooking, cleaning, or tending to the children. In these homes, there is a shared sense of responsibility and a recognition that both parents are contributing to the family’s well-being, not only in terms of income but also in the care of their children.

In my own view, I would advise a person in this situation to consider the strengths and circumstances of each individual. If one partner is more suited to the tasks of the home, or if the situation makes it more practical for one to remain at home—perhaps due to the nature of the work or the needs of the children—then that may be the path to follow. But it should never be a matter of one being lesser or of less value. Both roles are vital to the family.

I would also urge them to remain open to change. Circumstances may shift over time—perhaps a child grows older, or a new opportunity arises. What is best today may not be best tomorrow, and that is to be expected.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and thoughtful position, as I am asked to give counsel on a matter that, though new in its form, touches upon a concern as old as the family itself — the upbringing of children. You have told me that in this future society, the path to good education is paved with competition and early accomplishment, and that coaching, when carefully guided, can greatly improve a child's chances. This is a truth I know well, for in my own time, the value of a good education was often the key to opportunity, and those who could afford tutors or private instruction often gave their children an edge.

Now, the question is whether a parent should personally organize and supervise much of a child's free time, or whether it is better to allow the child to play freely, with only ordinary neighborhood supervision.

I must say, I see both paths with some understanding, though I lean more toward the latter. Let me explain.

In my time, we often said that a child should be given room to grow — to run, to play, to make mistakes, to learn from them. We believed that the world was a place of discovery, and that the best lessons were not always taught in books or by tutors. A child who learns to climb a tree, to build a fort, to make friends, to solve a problem on their own, is learning something far more valuable than any examination can measure.

That said, I do not dismiss the value of guidance. A parent's hand can be a helpful one, especially in shaping a child's habits, in encouraging them to work hard, and in helping them to see the value of discipline. But I believe that the line must be drawn carefully. If a child's every moment is planned and directed, there may come a time when they do not know how to think for themselves, or how to find joy in the simple things.
